newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bankers look to the future, close door on past.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bankers look to the future, close door on past.

text.p: Hundreds of bankers will converge near the sands of Waikiki this weekend looking to the future after closing the door on troubling issues of the past.
About 1,100 bankers are registered for the American Bankers Association convention set in Hawaii's capital city from Saturday through Oct. 8.
"This is not an industry that is trying to resolve major problems, this is an industry that is really looking toward the future," Mike ter Maat, senior economist at ABA, said.

One issue that had been hanging over the industry was resolved last week when Congress passed legislation to bolster the undercapitalized Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF), which insures deposits at thrifts.
Banks will pay more than $10 billion over 20 years to help defray interest payments on bonds issued in the late 1980s for the S&L bailout.
The industry is generally expected to stay on a profitable path, with analysts seeing few pitfalls ahead.
"The banking industry is about as well-positioned as it's ever been in history to improve profitability and grow," William Seidman, former chairman of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., said.
"Getting the SAIF thing behind them means that the merger trend can continue, which is going to help their efficiency," he said.
That legislation paves the way for banks and thrifts to merge their charters and essentially meld into one industry.
Charter merger will give "banks a great opportunity to modernise their basic operating authority," Seidman said.

Bankers will also make another push for legislation to further modernise the industry, but no one would make any predictions about whether the next Congress would be the one to repeal the Glass-Steagall Act.
Efforts to do away with that Depression-era law, which separates investment and commercial banking, have failed for decades.

But banks may get a smaller step in that direction if the Federal Reserve finalises a proposal that would increase the amount of securities underwriting that banks can conduct through securities subsidiaries.

The so-called "section 20" units currently can derive up to 10 percent of their revenue from underwriting in securities such as stocks and corporate bonds. The Fed proposal would lift that limit to 25 percent.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan will speak at the convention Saturday, along with FDIC Chairman Ricki Helfer and Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig.
Technology is also a focal point for banks looking to the future, with wide interest in how such developments such as stored-value cards and banking on the Internet may shape the future.

"The movement of electronic money will continue to be an ever increasing issue and we'll probably see some of these experiments begin to take wider form," Warren Heller, research director at VERIBANC Inc., said.
